metadata.title: How LLM Function Calling Works
notes: Register is Plain (runtime/prose/plain/PROSE.md), not Teardown: the six moves are sequenced across the sheet - stake first (B00/B01), wrong guess built then falsified (B02/B03), mechanism once with exactly ONE inference flag (B05), one running example planted early and paid off late (Boston, B00 -> B07/B08), failure modes in BOTH directions (B09), one compressible sentence to close (BVDT).
Plain does not judge the design - that is Teardown. No beat rates the design of function calling; the sheet explains how it works and stops.

beats.narration_text: Hi, my name is Prashanth, and this video is about how function calling lets a language model use real tools. Ask a model what the weather is in Boston right now. By itself, it cannot know that. And yet you have seen models answer that correctly, with a number in it. Something happened in between.

shot.visual_intent: COLD OPEN LAW - opens directly on the Claude UI, and the ask lands answered so ASK->RESULT begins at beat zero

output lines land in order: the tool request, then the tool result, then the sentence the viewer would actually see

props.command: What's the weather in Boston right now?
output: It's 41°F and overcast in Boston right now.

beats.narration_text: Function calling is how a model asks your program to run a tool, and then uses what comes back. That one distinction, asks rather than runs, is the whole subject of this video.

shot.new_visual_element: the overview written, reconsidered, and corrected on screen
shot.visual_intent: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW - the whole idea in one breath for a smart outsider; the correction IS the reel's misconception, the one the body dismantles

show.event: 0.8s of silence - the caret blinks on an empty cream page before the voice starts
writer types line one: 'Function calling is how a model'
types the WRONG verb 'runs' - it turns terracotta, marked for deletion
a full beat of hesitation, then 'runs' deletes
'asks your program to run' types in its place - the correction
final line completes: 'and then uses what comes back' - corrected sentence holds through the cut

props.text:
Function calling is how a model
runs a tool
and then uses what comes back.

beats.narration_text: Here is the guess almost everyone starts with. The model needed live weather, so the model went and got it: reached out to the internet, read a page, came back. It is a completely reasonable picture, and it is the one most people carry. Commit to it, or against it, now, before the next beat.

shot.new_visual_element: predict-card - the viewer commits before the reveal
shot.visual_intent: Plain move 2, build the wrong guess before the right one; the card holds the plausible-but-wrong model so it can be replaced rather than sit next to the correct one

the two candidate readings list in, ink on cream, neither highlighted

card holds still, giving the viewer real time to choose

props.question: The model “called a tool.” Who actually ran it — the model, or your program?
props.commit: commit to an answer before the next beat

beats.narration_text: If the model really fetched that weather, one thing would follow: your program would be optional. Turn your program off, and the answer would still arrive. It does not. Nothing arrives. A language model produces text, and only text. It holds no clock, no connection, no keys.

shot.new_visual_element: chip grid of the five things a language model does not have
shot.visual_intent: Plain move 2 payoff - break the wrong guess with one concrete falsifying case, then show what the model actually lacks as on-screen evidence (no-source-no-verdict)

show.event: five chips land in narration order: a clock, a network connection, your database, your API keys, permission to act
each chip greys as it lands - none is the accent, because none of them is available
caption types under the grid: a language model produces text and only text

props.caption: a language model has none of these — turn your program off and no answer arrives

beats.narration_text: So here is what actually happens, in four steps. One: you describe your tools to the model, in writing. Two: the model replies with a request, a tool name and arguments. Three: your program runs that tool. Four: you hand the result back, and the model writes the answer. Four steps. Hold onto them.

shot.new_visual_element: the four-stage round trip, labels only
shot.visual_intent: FRAMEWORK beat - presented in full BEFORE the worked example, and left as the reel's reference figure so B07 can visibly reuse it

show.event: stage 1 card lands top-left as the voice says 'one'
connector draws right; stage 2 card lands top-right on 'two'
connector draws down; stage 3 card lands bottom-right on 'three'
connector draws left; stage 4 card lands bottom-left on 'four'
the RETURN leg draws upward in dashed terracotta - stage 4 back into stage 1, the only accent in the frame
caption settles under the ring: one question, two model turns

stages.title: The model requests one
stages.sub: a tool name plus arguments, not an answer

stages.title: Your program runs it
stages.sub: your code, your keys, your network

stages.title: The result goes back
stages.sub: appended to the conversation, model runs again

props.caption: the fourth step feeds the first — which is why this is a loop, not a pipeline

beats.narration_text: Step one is the part people skip. You send the model a written description of each tool: its name, what it does, what arguments it takes. That description is just text in the conversation. When your question arrives, the model matches it against those descriptions. One flag: that matching is learned behaviour, not a lookup table. The description is your only steering wheel.

shot.new_visual_element: tool definitions flowing from your codebase into the model's context, one matching the ask
shot.visual_intent: Plain move 3 - the mechanism explained once, plainly, with EXACTLY ONE inference flag placed where 'learned behaviour' is doing real work

the question appears in the window's task line
get_weather checks off in terracotta as the match; the other two stay ink - one accent, so the match is unmistakable
settle line reads: the description is the steering wheel

props.arcCaption: sent as text, in the conversation

beats.narration_text: Let's put a real question through those four steps, and show every payload as it moves.

props.command: Trace the Boston weather question through all four steps. Show the exact payload at each one.

beats.narration_text: Boston. Step one: your tool list already includes get weather, taking a city. Step two: the model does not answer. It emits a request, get weather, city Boston. Step three: your code calls the real service and gets back forty-one degrees. Step four: that number goes back to the model, which writes the sentence you actually read.

shot.new_visual_element: the SAME four-stage figure, now carrying the real payload at each stage
shot.visual_intent: WORKED EXAMPLE - the example USES the framework figure from B04 rather than sitting beside it; each stage lights in turn as its payload lands

stages.title: The result goes back
stages.sub: the model runs a second time

props.caption: example values, shown to trace the mechanism — not a live reading

beats.narration_text: Here is the part that surprises people. The result does not go into some side channel. It gets appended to the conversation as a new message, and the model runs again on the longer conversation. One question, two model turns. The tool result is just more text the model reads.

shot.new_visual_element: the message list after one tool call, as real message objects
shot.visual_intent: the return leg made literal - the viewer READS the four messages while the voice reacts to them, so the evidence is on screen and not in the narration

message 2 (assistant, tool_use) lands - note it is the assistant's turn, and it contains a request
message 3 (user, tool_result) lands - the result arrives as a MESSAGE, in the same list
message 4 (assistant, text) lands - the second model turn, the answer
spark line holds: two turns, one question

props.title: the conversation, after one tool call

beats.narration_text: And it does not have to stop at one. If the first result is not enough, the model can request another tool, and another, each time on a longer conversation. That is all an agent is: this same four-step loop, run repeatedly, until the model has what it needs to answer. No new mechanism. Just more turns.

shot.new_visual_element: the conversation stack growing one round per tool call
shot.visual_intent: extends the return leg from B04/B07 into repetition, and lands the function-calling-to-agents bridge without introducing a new mechanism

show.event: round 1 card stacks in: ask, request, result, answer attempt
round 2 stacks beneath it - the conversation is visibly longer than in round 1
round 3 stacks in terracotta, the one accent, marked 'until it has enough'
caption settles: an agent is this loop, run repeatedly

layers.sub: one tool requested, one result returned — not enough yet

layers.title: round 2
layers.sub: the model asks for a second tool, on a longer conversation

layers.title: round 3
layers.sub: enough context at last — it answers

props.caption: an agent is not a new mechanism — it is this same four-step loop, run until it has enough

beats.narration_text: Now the limits, both ways. A tool call that succeeds does not prove the model understood your question: it can call the right tool with wrong arguments and return a confident, wrong answer. And a tool the model never calls does not prove the tool was wrong. Usually the description was vague. The description is where this breaks.

shot.new_visual_element: binary branch - the two failure directions, resolved by the same cause
shot.visual_intent: Plain move 5 - state what a POSITIVE result does not prove and what a NEGATIVE result does not prove; naming only one direction would overstate reliability

show.event: the question splits into two branches from a single node
left branch fills: the call succeeded, arguments wrong, answer confident and wrong
right branch fills: no call made, tool was fine, description was vague
both branches converge on one resolver card in terracotta: the description
resolver holds - the single lever behind both failures

data.question: The model called your tool. Did it understand the question?

branches.label: it called the tool
branches.detail: succeeded, but with wrong arguments — a confident, wrong answer
branches.fix: a success does not prove understanding

branches.label: it never called it
branches.detail: the tool was fine; the model could not tell when to reach for it
branches.fix: a silence does not prove the tool is wrong

resolver.label: the description
resolver.detail: both failures trace back to how the tool was described — the one part you control

beats.narration_text: So, the one sentence worth repeating: the model never runs anything. It writes a request, your program runs it, and the result comes back as more conversation. Everything else about function calling follows from that, including agents. And the part you actually control is the description you wrote in step one.

shot.new_visual_element: artifact page holding the compressible sentence
shot.visual_intent: Plain move 6 - close on one sentence that stays true if it is the only thing repeated secondhand; it compresses the DISTINCTION, not the topic

show.event: artifact page opens in the Claude window
the one-line claim lands first, largest on the page
the three mechanical consequences list under it, in order
the last line holds alone: what you own is the description

artifactLines: It writes a request. Your program runs it.
The result returns as another message — not a side channel.
So one question costs two model turns, not one.
What you own: the tool description. That is the steering wheel.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: describe one task at my job that needs live data, then write a tool definition for it, name, description and arguments, and show me the exact request you'd emit for one real example. Then check three things in the answer. Does the description say when to use the tool, not just what it does. Are the arguments things your program can actually supply. And is the request valid for your example. Pause here and run it.

shot.new_visual_element: the composer with the viewer's prompt, and the three-point rubric beside it
shot.visual_intent: HANDOFF LAW plus nopunt SCAFFOLDED TASK - the prompt is read aloud verbatim and discussed, and the rubric gives the viewer a way to judge the output rather than just admire it

props.command: Describe one task at my job that needs live data. Then write a tool definition for it — name, description, and arguments — and show me the exact request you'd emit for one real example.
output: Check the answer against three things:
1. does the description say WHEN to use the tool, not just what it does?
2. are the arguments things your program can actually supply?
3. is the request valid for your own example?

beats.narration_text: That's function calling. Thanks for watching.
